author: Rinehart
text:
I said hiccup to mean kink but imply it is not important.

From what you have written about wanting E to be THE FL. I would say you have no trade here.

Word of advice --- examine every FL on the lowest possible time frame to get the proper boundaries.

Wouldn't a HTF FL be a LTF Flag?

The other thing is this is one of those questions you kind of have to figure out yourself. If you put a chart in front of us, we can answer it case by case. On the other hand, if you are talking about an abstract situation, it depends because each situation is a little different. A break of support on weekly will create a FL. That HTF FL is still comprised of LTF zones. When I'm examining price to put on a trade, I examine my FL on the lowest time frame available to get he boundaries right. Your job is to find the important ones.

author: hoeschec
text:
Here is an analysis of my USD-JPY trade today: I'll start by posting the final chart, and then I will attach each of the charts showing my analysis that led up to taking the trade.

Part 1:Look left to draw the order flow as price engulfs, retraces, and forms a swap zone.

Notice how Box 3 was drawn... paying close attention to the inner FL (lower scale).

"A" shows where buyers entered the market to push price up to "B", where price took the remaining supply in Box 3 (which is a swap zone). I used the low @ "A" as the basis for Box 4, which ends up being the reason for my trade. Point C & D was confirmation that a FO would happen in to Box 4 (B&C is a RS bounce from the edge of Box 4). But, I only took the trade because of what happened in the PA between "A" and "B", specifically that B took the LQ in Box 3, which is a swap zone. No engulf happened above Box 3, which tells me all of the seller LQ was taken.

As you can see, once I complete the order flow analysis to the left, the entry is really easy. In this case, my SL was tiny.

This trade is not my typical setup, as the primary reason for taking the short was not a return to a fakeout. That said, the methodology is very similar. In my opinion, the most important part of this trade, and the reason there was sufficient order flow to bounce price, was because of how price reacted to Box 3, a swap zone. It is the same scenario for FO trades... I want to see the FO happen to a specific area of LQ at a swap zone without engulfing

author: hoeschec
text:
Interesting Trade that I took last night on USD-CHF... great example to share. This was 17:R

I tried to clearly show where my entry and exit was. For some reason, my platform places arrows in odd places. The dotted red line is more accurate to show my entry/exit. I closed out the trade in the red circle area. My SL was about 3 pips.

Something I want to share...I have been making some changes to my strategy lately. I am becoming MUCH more interested in the approach price takes before it reaches my entry. I am learning that is more important than finding the bounce points. For example: the yellow box is pretty easy to find/draw. It's just carefully drawing FL boxes... simple.

We find areas like this all over the charts, and often they bounce price. But, we also see these FL's fail.

I am learning that whether a FL will hold depends on prices approach to the level. I want to see a structured attempt at creating supply/demand just below/above my FL box (my entry of interest). I want to see how price approaches my box, but I want price to FAIL to hit the zone. Then, I want to see a deep retrace back to some strong pocket of Liquidity before price begins to rise/drop to the entry point. These supply/demand created levels that fail to hit the entry target act as a perfect trap for traders to get in on the "breakout".

This takes some time to find on the charts... I am still practicing it. But, this USD-CHF is a perfect example. I would not have taken this trade if price hadn't formed that supply level to the immediate left of my actual entry. When I saw that false supply form, I added my limit orders and woke up to a 17:R trade!

Focus on thinking like a predator... rewire your brain to see the tricks for LQ and trading gets easier.

Hope this helps!!e

author: hoeschec
text:
I was doing some practicing today and came across this example on EUR-USD. For those who read my journal, you will know I normally focus on trading the RT to a FO. This is my main strategy, but over the past month I've been studying FO's carefully...to better understand them.

Trading the FO as it forms would be the ideal strategy... limited risk; lots of upside.

I was wondering why price didn't bounce in the blue box (selling when price first hits the blue box). Instead, price blew right through the zone. There is even a supply zone for a perfect fakeout... but no bounce.

I looked at a higher TF chart, and the answer became clear to me: price was coming from a higher TF FO. See the chart Below:

On a higher TF scale, this was a FO to trap LQ for a push up... and that's a very bad time to sell. On the lower TF, this original short (at FL 3) looked good. But when you see the big picture, you see the real FO happened at FL "A".

Summary: make you aren't buying or selling against the higher time frames.
